item.content:encoded:
The University of California, Berkeley, through the Haas School of Business and its Center for Social Sector Leadership (CSL), is inviting qualified professionals to apply for the Philanthropy Fellow, Civil Society and Leadership position with the David and Lucile Packard Foundation.

This full-time professional opportunity offers an exciting pathway for emerging leaders interested in philanthropy, civil society, nonprofit organizations, strategic grantmaking, social impact, research, evaluation, leadership, and international development. The successful candidate will work with the Packard Foundation’s Civil Society and Leadership team while receiving professional development, coaching, mentorship, and institutional support from UC Berkeley’s Center for Social Sector Leadership.

The position is based at the David and Lucile Packard Foundation in Los Altos, California, with the Foundation currently operating on a hybrid schedule in which staff work from the office on Tuesdays and Wednesdays.

The role provides an opportunity to gain practical experience in strategic philanthropy while contributing to research, evaluation and learning, strategy implementation, grantmaking, knowledge management, project management, and engagement with nonprofit organizations and other stakeholders.

Opportunity Overview

  • Position: Philanthropy Fellow, Civil Society and Leadership
  • Job ID: 88658
  • Reference Number: 5257C
  • Employer: University of California, Berkeley
  • Partner Organization: The David and Lucile Packard Foundation
  • Department: Haas School of Business / Center for Social Sector Leadership
  • Team: Civil Society and Leadership Initiative
  • Location: Los Altos, California, USA
  • Work Arrangement: Hybrid
  • Employment Type: Full-time
  • Hours: 40 hours per week
  • Salary: $78,435 to $90,000 per year
  • Application Materials: Resume and cover letter
  • First Review Date: September 22, 2026
  • Visa Sponsorship: Not a visa opportunity

About UC Berkeley

The University of California, Berkeley is one of the world’s leading public research universities. Founded in 1868, Berkeley has developed a global reputation for academic excellence, innovation, research, public service, and social impact.

The university describes its community as one built around openness, freedom, belonging, equity, and opportunity. Its faculty, students, researchers, and staff include internationally recognized scholars and leaders, and the institution has played a significant role in intellectual, economic, scientific, and social progress in California, the United States, and beyond.

For employees, Berkeley emphasizes continuous learning and professional development. Full-time staff employees receive support for professional growth, including paid professional development time and access to colleague communities and employee resource groups.

The Philanthropy Fellow position is situated within this broader environment of learning, leadership, innovation, and public impact.

About the Haas School of Business

The UC Berkeley Haas School of Business is the academic home supporting this fellowship partnership. Haas is known for a culture that encourages innovation, collaboration, leadership, and continuous learning.

The school’s workplace culture is organized around four defining leadership principles:

  1. Question the Status Quo
  2. Confidence Without Attitude
  3. Students Always
  4. Beyond Yourself

These principles are particularly relevant to the Philanthropy Fellow role because the position requires someone who can think strategically, work collaboratively, approach complex social challenges with curiosity, and contribute to initiatives designed to strengthen civil society.

Haas also supports flexible working arrangements, although specific arrangements depend on the responsibilities of each role and are determined in partnership with supervisors.

About the David and Lucile Packard Foundation

The David and Lucile Packard Foundation was established in 1964 by David and Lucile Packard. The Foundation works with people and communities to develop enduring solutions that contribute to just societies and a healthy, resilient natural world.

Over the years, the Foundation has supported organizations and leaders working across a range of important areas, including:

  • Science
  • Ocean and land conservation
  • Climate change
  • Women’s reproductive health and rights
  • Children, families, and communities
  • Civil society
  • Social justice
  • Community well-being

The Foundation’s work involves partnerships with organizations and leaders in the United States and internationally.

For someone seeking to build a career in philanthropy, nonprofit leadership, international development, or social impact, the opportunity provides exposure to how a major philanthropic institution works with grantees, partners, experts, and other stakeholders to address complex societal challenges.

About the Civil Society and Leadership Initiative

The Philanthropy Fellow will work within the Foundation’s Civil Society and Leadership (CSL) Initiative.

The Packard Foundation’s strategic framework recognizes civil society as an important component of achieving its broader goals and contributing to a just society. The CSL Initiative therefore focuses on strengthening civil society organizations, supporting resilient civil society ecosystems, and promoting a safe and thriving civic space.

The initiative operates under the Foundation’s Just Societies goal while supporting work connected to the Foundation’s other major goals and geographic areas of operation.

This makes the fellowship particularly relevant to professionals interested in questions surrounding:

  • Civil society development
  • Nonprofit organizations
  • Civic space
  • Social justice
  • Philanthropy
  • Organizational resilience
  • Strategic grantmaking
  • Public policy
  • Community development
  • Social impact
  • Evaluation and learning
  • International development

What Is the UC Berkeley–Packard Foundation Philanthropy Fellowship?

The partnership between UC Berkeley and the Packard Foundation is designed to strengthen the future of philanthropy and civil society by introducing recent graduates and emerging professionals from diverse academic and professional backgrounds to the philanthropic and nonprofit sectors.

The fellowship has two major objectives.

1. Developing the next generation of philanthropic leaders

The program provides participants with professional-level exposure to philanthropy and nonprofit work. Through direct involvement in Foundation activities, the Fellow can develop knowledge and skills that may support a future career in philanthropy, civil society, nonprofit leadership, social impact, policy, research, or related fields.

2. Bringing fresh perspectives to the Packard Foundation

The partnership also allows the Foundation to benefit from new ideas, skills, experiences, and perspectives brought by the Fellows.

The selected Fellow will join a cohort of four other fellows working across different Foundation areas, including environment and science, families and communities, and global reproductive health.

The fellowship cohort will participate in quarterly activities, creating additional opportunities for learning, collaboration, networking, and professional development.

Where Will the Fellow Work?

The Fellow will be based at the David and Lucile Packard Foundation in Los Altos, California.

The Foundation currently uses a hybrid work schedule, with staff attending the office on Tuesdays and Wednesdays.

The position therefore combines professional experience within a major philanthropic organization with the resources and support of UC Berkeley’s Center for Social Sector Leadership.

Key Responsibilities of the Philanthropy Fellow

The selected Fellow will have a broad range of responsibilities involving research, evaluation, strategy, grantmaking, project management, knowledge management, stakeholder engagement, and professional learning.

1. Monitoring, Evaluation, and Learning

The Fellow will support CSL’s monitoring, evaluation, and learning activities.

This may include:

  • Supporting research projects
  • Coordinating internal learning processes
  • Contributing to evaluation activities
  • Helping the team assess progress
  • Supporting strategic reflection
  • Contributing to the Foundation’s mid-strategy reflection for 2027–2028

This responsibility makes research, analytical thinking, organization, and the ability to interpret evidence particularly important.

2. Strategy Development and Implementation

The Fellow will work with the CSL team to help inform and refine organizational strategy.

Responsibilities may include:

  • Conducting research
  • Analyzing relevant information
  • Supporting strategic discussions
  • Facilitating team deliberations
  • Identifying relevant trends and issues
  • Contributing research that informs decision-making

The role therefore requires more than administrative ability. Applicants should be comfortable examining complex issues, identifying relevant evidence, synthesizing information, and communicating findings clearly.

3. Grantmaking Support

The Fellow will work with a Program Officer and Program Associate to support grantmaking within a CSL portfolio.

This provides an opportunity to gain practical exposure to how philanthropic organizations identify priorities, engage with organizations, develop grant-related materials, and support initiatives designed to strengthen civil society.

4. Project and Event Management

The Fellow will project-manage important initiatives and events for the CSL team.

Examples include supporting strategy sessions held during organizational retreats.

This requires strong organizational skills and the ability to coordinate multiple activities, deadlines, people, and deliverables.

5. Knowledge Management

Knowledge management is another important component of the position.

The Fellow will help maintain and improve the team’s knowledge-management infrastructure and identify efficient ways to store and analyze different types of information and data.

Applicants should therefore be comfortable working with information systems, organizing knowledge, identifying patterns, and developing streamlined processes.

6. Support for Program Officers

The Fellow will provide support to relevant program officers.

This can include:

  • Preparing materials for meetings
  • Preparing meeting agendas
  • Supporting grantee meetings
  • Supporting field convenings
  • Participating in meetings with grantees
  • Participating in site visits
  • Preparing meeting summaries
  • Managing follow-up actions
  • Supporting other program-related activities

These responsibilities require strong written communication, attention to detail, interpersonal skills, and the ability to work professionally with different stakeholders.

7. Stakeholder Engagement

The Fellow may interact with a broad range of individuals and organizations, including:

  • Foundation program staff
  • Evaluation staff
  • Grantees
  • Funding partners
  • Government agencies
  • Content experts
  • Civil society organizations
  • Other relevant partners

This exposure can provide valuable insight into how strategic philanthropy operates in practice.

8. Travel and Conferences

The role may involve travel to meet new and existing partners and to participate in conferences relevant to the Civil Society and Leadership Initiative and the Fellow’s professional development goals.

This means the position may provide opportunities to learn directly from organizations, practitioners, experts, and other professionals working in civil society and philanthropy.

9. Foundation-Wide and University Activities

The Fellow will also participate in Foundation-wide activities that are relevant to their work and professional objectives.

They will have opportunities to engage with both University and Foundation communities and participate in professional development opportunities related to their responsibilities.

10. Professional Learning and Growth

Professional development is an important part of the position.

The Fellow is expected to contribute positively to a team environment that promotes belonging and collaboration and to demonstrate the Haas School of Business leadership principles.

The successful candidate will also be expected to complete required training and take advantage of relevant learning opportunities.

Professional Development Benefits

One of the distinctive features of this opportunity is the professional development support attached to the fellowship.

The Fellow will receive support from the Center for Social Sector Leadership at UC Berkeley, including context about the philanthropic sector, access to resources, and personal coaching and supervision.

The fellowship also includes a professional development budget.

This budget can support activities such as:

  • Attending conferences related to philanthropy
  • Participating in civil society conferences
  • Taking relevant workshops
  • Attending seminars
  • Receiving professional career coaching
  • Developing specific skills
  • Building knowledge relevant to future career objectives

For early-career professionals, this additional development component can make the role particularly valuable because the position is designed not only around immediate responsibilities but also around long-term leadership development.

Required Qualifications

Applicants are expected to demonstrate a combination of education, professional experience, analytical ability, communication skills, and knowledge of civil society.

Educational and professional experience

Candidates should have:

  • At least two to three years of experience and/or graduate-level education in a related field.
  • At least two years of experience working in a full-time professional position.
  • A bachelor’s degree in a related area or equivalent experience and training.
  • Experience working in civil society organizations.

The wording of the requirements means applicants should carefully demonstrate how their education and professional background relate to civil society, philanthropy, nonprofit organizations, research, public policy, social impact, or another relevant field.

Strategic thinking and research

Candidates should be strong strategic thinkers and researchers.

They should be able to:

  • Conduct research
  • Analyze information
  • Understand studies
  • Interpret complex material
  • Identify relevant evidence
  • Synthesize findings
  • Apply research to practical decision-making

Understanding of civil society

Applicants should demonstrate awareness of current threats and challenges facing civil society.

This may include understanding issues affecting nonprofit organizations, civic space, social movements, community organizations, institutional resilience, governance, or other factors influencing the ability of civil society actors to operate effectively.

Knowledge management

Applicants should have experience or demonstrated ability in developing systems and practices for effective knowledge management.

This is important because the position involves working with multiple types of information and helping the team store, organize, retrieve, and analyze knowledge efficiently.

Communication skills

Excellent communication skills are required.

Applicants should be able to:

  • Write clearly
  • Communicate complex ideas
  • Structure analysis
  • Synthesize information
  • Prepare reports
  • Present findings
  • Communicate effectively with different stakeholders

Both oral and written communication are emphasized in the job description.

Interpersonal and teamwork skills

The role involves collaboration with Foundation staff, grantees, government agencies, experts, funding partners, and other stakeholders.

Applicants therefore need strong interpersonal skills and the ability to work effectively as part of a team.

Initiative and project management

The successful candidate should demonstrate strong initiative and be capable of managing multiple tasks and projects across diverse subject areas.

The role involves balancing research, grantmaking support, meetings, events, knowledge management, stakeholder engagement, and professional development.

Judgment and decision-making

Candidates should be comfortable operating in ambiguous situations.

The position requires the ability to use judgment, make sound decisions, and move projects forward even when complete information may not be available.

Responsible use of artificial intelligence

Another notable requirement is the ability to creatively and ethically use artificial intelligence to support strategy and learning.

Applicants should therefore be prepared to demonstrate that they understand how AI can be used responsibly to improve research, analysis, knowledge management, learning, and strategic work while maintaining appropriate ethical standards.

Preferred Qualifications

The following qualifications are preferred but are not listed as mandatory requirements.

Experience strengthening civil society

Applicants with experience working in organizations focused on strengthening civil society, enabling conditions, or threats affecting civil society may be particularly competitive.

International experience

Experience working internationally is preferred.

This could be especially relevant for applicants who have worked across countries, regions, international organizations, global nonprofits, development institutions, or cross-border civil society initiatives.

Language skills

High proficiency in conversational Spanish, French, or Bahasa Indonesian is preferred.

Applicants who possess one or more of these language skills should highlight them clearly in their application materials.

Graduate-level education

Graduate-level education or comparable experience in areas such as:

  • International development
  • Public policy
  • Public health
  • Social science
  • Law
  • Related disciplines

is preferred.

Salary and Benefits

The position is a 100% full-time career position, requiring approximately 40 hours per week.

The budgeted annual salary range is:

$78,435 to $90,000 per year.

The position is also eligible for UC Benefits.

The exact salary offered to a successful candidate will depend on factors including qualifications, experience, skills, knowledge, abilities, education, internal equity, and other organizational considerations.

The University notes that it is not typical for an individual to be offered compensation at or near the top of the posted range.

Is This a Visa Opportunity?

No.

The job description explicitly states:

This is not a visa opportunity.

International applicants should therefore carefully consider their existing authorization and eligibility to work in the United States before applying.

Application Requirements

Applicants are required to submit:

  1. A resume
  2. A cover letter

Because the position emphasizes research, strategic thinking, civil society experience, communication, and professional judgment, applicants should ensure that their application materials clearly demonstrate these areas rather than simply listing general duties.

A strong application should make it easy for the hiring team to see the connection between the applicant’s background and the responsibilities of the Philanthropy Fellow position.

How to Strengthen Your Application

Candidates interested in this opportunity can consider emphasizing the following areas in their resume and cover letter:

Demonstrate civil society experience

Clearly explain your experience with civil society organizations, nonprofits, community organizations, social-impact initiatives, advocacy organizations, or related institutions.

Show research and analytical ability

Rather than simply stating that you have research skills, provide evidence of situations where you conducted research, analyzed information, synthesized findings, or supported strategic decisions.

Highlight strategic thinking

Explain how your work has contributed to strategy development, planning, organizational improvement, program design, evaluation, or decision-making.

Emphasize communication

The role requires outstanding written and oral communication. Highlight experience preparing reports, research documents, presentations, briefing materials, meeting summaries, strategic documents, or other professional communications.

Explain your project-management experience

Show how you have coordinated multiple tasks, projects, meetings, events, stakeholders, or deadlines.

Highlight knowledge management

If you have created information-management systems, databases, documentation processes, digital repositories, research libraries, reporting systems, or organizational knowledge systems, make these achievements visible in your application.

Demonstrate responsible AI use

Applicants should be prepared to explain practical examples of how they have used AI ethically to improve research, learning, analysis, communication, or strategy.

Connect your goals to philanthropy

Because the fellowship is designed to introduce emerging leaders to philanthropy and civil society, applicants should clearly communicate why they want to develop a career in these areas and how the fellowship fits into their longer-term professional goals.

Background Check and Other Employment Conditions

The position is designated as requiring fingerprinting and a background check because of the nature of its responsibilities.

UC Berkeley states that it hires individuals with conviction histories and reviews such information in the context of the responsibilities of the position. Employment may be made contingent upon successfully completing the required background check.

The final candidate who accepts a conditional offer will also be required to disclose certain misconduct-related matters, including specified administrative or judicial decisions, allegations, proceedings, investigations, or appeals involving misconduct within the applicable seven-year period.

The job is also covered by the collective bargaining agreement between the United Auto Workers (UAW) and the University of California Regents for RP.

Equal Employment Opportunity

The University of California is an Equal Opportunity Employer.

Qualified applicants receive consideration without regard to protected characteristics including race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, national origin, disability, age, protected veteran status, or other protected status under applicable law.

This means applicants from diverse backgrounds are encouraged to consider the opportunity provided they meet the stated qualifications and employment requirements.

Who Should Apply?

This opportunity is particularly suitable for professionals and emerging leaders who want to build or strengthen careers in areas such as:

  • Philanthropy
  • Civil society
  • Nonprofit management
  • Social impact
  • International development
  • Public policy
  • Public health
  • Social sciences
  • Law
  • Research and evaluation
  • Strategic grantmaking
  • Community development
  • Organizational learning
  • Civic space and civil society resilience

The position is especially relevant to candidates who already have professional experience in civil society organizations and who can demonstrate strong research, analytical, communication, interpersonal, project-management, and strategic-thinking abilities.

APPLY HERE

Eligibility by Country and Continent

The job description does not specify a restricted list of countries or continents from which applicants may apply.

However, there is an important geographic and immigration consideration: the position is based in California, United States, and the employer explicitly states that this is not a visa opportunity.

Therefore, applicants from different countries may potentially submit an application if they otherwise meet the requirements, but international candidates should independently ensure that they already have the necessary legal authorization to work in the United States.

The employer’s equal opportunity statement also indicates that qualified applicants are considered without discrimination based on race, color, national origin, and other protected characteristics.

Deadline and Application Review Date

The job posting lists the First Review Date as September 22, 2026.

Applicants should therefore aim to submit their applications before September 22, 2026 to ensure they are considered during the initial review period.

The job description does not provide a conventional final application deadline in the information supplied. For that reason, September 22, 2026 should be treated as the key date stated in the announcement.

Why This Opportunity Stands Out

The UC Berkeley–Packard Foundation Philanthropy Fellow position combines several elements that can be valuable for someone developing a career in the social-impact sector.

First, the Fellow gains direct exposure to a major philanthropic foundation and its grantmaking activities.

Second, the position combines practical work with structured professional development.

Third, the Fellow receives support from UC Berkeley’s Center for Social Sector Leadership.

Fourth, the role provides exposure to research, monitoring and evaluation, strategy, grantmaking, knowledge management, stakeholder engagement, and civil society issues.

Finally, joining a cohort of other fellows creates an additional environment for peer learning and professional networking.

Visit HERE to learn more about the UC Berkeley–Packard Foundation Philanthropy Fellow 2026.

Conclusion

The UC Berkeley–Packard Foundation Philanthropy Fellow, Civil Society and Leadership opportunity is a significant professional opportunity for candidates interested in the intersection of philanthropy, civil society, nonprofit organizations, strategic grantmaking, research, and social impact.

Based at the David and Lucile Packard Foundation in Los Altos, California, the successful candidate will contribute to meaningful work involving strategy, monitoring and evaluation, grantmaking, research, knowledge management, project management, stakeholder engagement, and organizational learning.

The position offers a full-time salary of $78,435 to $90,000 per year, UC benefits, professional coaching, a professional development budget, conference and training opportunities, and exposure to both the Foundation and UC Berkeley communities.

Candidates should pay close attention to the experience and skills requirements, particularly the emphasis on civil society experience, strategic research, knowledge management, communication, teamwork, initiative, judgment, and ethical use of AI.

The first review date is September 22, 2026, so qualified candidates should prepare their resume and cover letter and submit their applications as early as possible. International candidates should also note that the position is explicitly not a visa opportunity and should confirm their existing U.S. work authorization before applying.

item.content:encoded:
The 2027 Tools Competition is now open, inviting innovators, education technology developers, researchers, entrepreneurs, organisations and other solution-builders to propose tools and public infrastructure that can improve learning, teaching and access to opportunity.

The competition supports education technology innovation that uses digital technology, data, artificial intelligence and learning science to address urgent challenges facing learners and educators. Its seventh cycle comes at a time when artificial intelligence is becoming increasingly common in education, work and everyday life, creating new opportunities while also raising important questions about trust, safety, privacy, effectiveness and responsible implementation.

Rather than rewarding technology simply because it is new, the 2027 Tools Competition seeks proposals that demonstrate how tools can produce meaningful results in real-world learning environments. Strong proposals should explain how their solutions can be responsibly used, trusted, sustained and adapted to the needs of learners, educators and institutions.

The Tools Competition is a programme of Renaissance Philanthropy and is organised by The Learning Agency.

About the 2027 Tools Competition

The Tools Competition is a multi-million-dollar funding opportunity focused on education technology innovation. It supports tools and public infrastructure that use digital technology, big data and learning science to respond to pressing needs across education and workforce development.

The 2027 competition recognises that technology access alone does not automatically improve learning outcomes. A tool must be relevant to the learning context, easy to use, inclusive, evidence-informed and designed with the realities of learners and educators in mind.

The competition therefore encourages proposals that address questions such as:

  • Does the tool help learners understand what they know and what they still need to learn?
  • Does it provide timely and useful support?
  • Does it strengthen teaching practice rather than create unnecessary burdens?
  • Does it make learning more engaging, practical and learner-driven?
  • Does it help individuals navigate education-to-work transitions?
  • Does it improve the availability of high-quality education data?
  • Does it protect privacy, promote safety and support responsible technology use?
  • Can the solution be sustained and used effectively in real learning environments?

The strongest proposals will be those that demonstrate not only what technology or artificial intelligence can do, but also how the proposed solution can be implemented responsibly and generate meaningful benefits.

Why the Competition Matters

Artificial intelligence and digital tools are rapidly changing how people learn, work and access information. Many learners are already using generative AI to complete assignments, improve efficiency, understand difficult concepts and support their learning.

However, the increasing use of AI in education also creates challenges. Learners may not always know whether information generated by AI is accurate. Educators may lack guidance on how to integrate AI into instruction. Institutions may face concerns about privacy, unequal access, bias, academic integrity and the long-term effects of technology on learning.

The 2027 Tools Competition responds to this changing environment by encouraging the development of tools that are grounded in evidence and designed around actual learning needs.

The competition places particular emphasis on solutions that:

  • Improve the quality and usefulness of learning experiences.
  • Support educators in delivering effective instruction.
  • Provide inclusive and actionable information about student progress.
  • Help learners become more independent and confident.
  • Connect education with real-world opportunities.
  • Strengthen the infrastructure needed for future education research and development.
  • Integrate safety, privacy and responsibility into design and implementation.

This approach moves beyond technology for its own sake. It focuses on whether a tool can make education more effective, equitable, engaging and responsive.

2027 Tools Competition Tracks

The 2027 Tools Competition features four main tracks. These tracks cover K–12 education, postsecondary learning, the transition from education to work, and the development of high-quality datasets.

Applicants should review the tracks carefully and select the one that most closely matches the purpose, users and intended impact of their tool or idea.

1. Strengthening Teaching

The Strengthening Teaching track focuses on tools that improve instructional effectiveness while also making the teaching profession more sustainable.

Teachers often face multiple demands, including lesson planning, assessment, classroom management, administrative responsibilities, reporting and adapting instruction to different learner needs. Technology can help reduce unnecessary workload and provide educators with better information for making instructional decisions.

This track seeks tools that can support teachers in meaningful and practical ways. Proposed solutions should demonstrate how they can improve teaching quality, support professional practice and contribute to a more sustainable teaching environment.

Potential areas of focus may include:

  • Tools that support lesson planning and instructional preparation.
  • Systems that help educators identify student learning needs.
  • Platforms that provide timely instructional feedback.
  • Resources that improve classroom engagement.
  • Tools that reduce repetitive administrative work.
  • Solutions that support differentiated instruction.
  • Technologies that help teachers access and use evidence.
  • Tools that strengthen collaboration and professional learning.

A strong proposal for this track should explain how the tool supports educators without replacing professional judgement or adding unnecessary complexity.

Applicants can learn more through the official Strengthening Teaching track page:
Explore the Strengthening Teaching track

2. Reimagining Assessment

The Reimagining Assessment track focuses on tools that strengthen K–12 assessment by providing more continuous, actionable and inclusive information about student learning.

Traditional assessments may provide only a limited picture of what students know at a particular point in time. The competition encourages solutions that help educators and learners understand progress more continuously and use assessment information to improve learning.

Tools under this track may support the collection, interpretation and use of learning evidence in ways that are timely and useful.

Potential areas of focus may include:

  • Formative assessment tools.
  • Systems that identify learning gaps.
  • Platforms that provide immediate feedback.
  • Inclusive assessment approaches for diverse learners.
  • Tools that help teachers adjust instruction.
  • Solutions that make assessment more meaningful and less burdensome.
  • Technologies that provide clearer information about student progress.
  • Assessment tools that support personalised learning pathways.

Successful proposals should explain how the tool can produce reliable information and how that information can be used to improve learning outcomes.

Applicants can learn more through the official Reimagining Assessment track page:
Explore the Reimagining Assessment track

3. Navigating Postsecondary Learning and Work

The Navigating Postsecondary Learning and Work track focuses on tools that help learners build the skills, relationships, information and support needed to navigate education and employment in an increasingly AI-driven world.

The transition from secondary education to higher education, vocational training or employment can be difficult. Learners may need help identifying suitable programmes, developing relevant skills, finding mentors, understanding career pathways, building professional networks and making informed decisions.

This track seeks solutions that support learners during these transition points and help them connect education with real-world opportunities.

Potential areas of focus may include:

  • Career exploration and guidance tools.
  • Platforms connecting learners with mentors or professionals.
  • Tools that help students identify skills gaps.
  • Systems supporting postsecondary planning.
  • Resources that connect learners to internships, apprenticeships or jobs.
  • Tools that help learners build professional networks.
  • Technologies that support career readiness.
  • Platforms that improve access to information about education and work opportunities.
  • Solutions that help learners make informed decisions in changing labour markets.

Proposals should demonstrate how the tool can help learners navigate uncertainty with greater clarity, confidence and connection.

Applicants can learn more through the official Navigating Postsecondary Learning and Work track page:
Explore the Navigating Postsecondary Learning and Work track

4. Building Better Datasets

The Building Better Datasets track focuses on high-quality education datasets that can support future research, product development and innovation.

Data is essential for understanding learning, evaluating educational tools and developing systems that respond to the needs of diverse learners. However, education datasets may be incomplete, difficult to access, poorly documented or insufficiently representative of different populations and learning environments.

This track encourages the development of datasets that capture the diversity of learners, educational contexts and learning settings.

High-quality datasets may help researchers and developers:

  • Study learning patterns and outcomes.
  • Improve education technology tools.
  • Develop and evaluate artificial intelligence systems.
  • Understand differences across learning environments.
  • Support evidence-based education policy.
  • Improve the inclusiveness and reliability of educational research.
  • Identify gaps in existing education data.
  • Develop tools that are more responsive to real-world needs.

Applicants should explain the value of the proposed dataset, the population or learning context it represents, how the data will be collected or developed, and how privacy, consent, security and responsible use will be addressed.

Applicants can learn more through the official Building Better Datasets track page:
Explore the Building Better Datasets track

What Types of Proposals Are Encouraged?

The competition is intended for proposals that address important challenges in learning, teaching and opportunity. While the specific requirements may differ by track, strong proposals are likely to demonstrate several important qualities.

Evidence-informed design

Proposals should be grounded in relevant research, learning science, user experience evidence or practical knowledge of the problem being addressed. Applicants should explain why the proposed solution is likely to work and what evidence supports its approach.

Clear understanding of the target users

Applicants should identify who will use or benefit from the tool. Depending on the track, target users may include:

  • K–12 students.
  • Teachers and school leaders.
  • Postsecondary students.
  • Adult learners.
  • Career seekers.
  • Researchers.
  • Education institutions.
  • Workforce development organisations.
  • Policymakers.
  • Developers and education technology providers.

A strong proposal should demonstrate an understanding of the needs, constraints and experiences of the intended users.

Real-world usefulness

The competition is focused on tools that can function in real learning environments. Applicants should explain how their proposed solution will be used in practice and what problem it will solve.

Proposals should avoid focusing only on technical novelty. They should demonstrate how the tool will create practical value for learners, educators, institutions or researchers.

Responsible technology use

Safety, privacy and responsibility are central to the 2027 competition. Applicants should consider how their tool will protect users and avoid potential harm.

Relevant considerations may include:

  • Data privacy.
  • Informed consent.
  • Data security.
  • Bias and fairness.
  • Accessibility.
  • Transparency.
  • Responsible artificial intelligence.
  • Protection of children and vulnerable users.
  • Appropriate human oversight.
  • Accountability in design and implementation.

Potential for sustainability and scale

Strong proposals should consider how the tool can be maintained, adopted and sustained beyond an initial pilot. Applicants may need to explain the resources, partnerships, infrastructure or implementation strategies required for long-term use.

Who Should Consider Applying?

The competition may be relevant to a broad range of individuals and organisations working on education technology, learning science, digital infrastructure and workforce development.

Potential applicants may include:

  • Education technology startups.
  • Non-profit organisations.
  • Researchers and research teams.
  • Universities and academic institutions.
  • Education-focused companies.
  • Developers and technology innovators.
  • Social enterprises.
  • Data scientists.
  • Learning designers.
  • Educators developing innovative tools.
  • Organisations working in K–12 education.
  • Organisations supporting postsecondary learners.
  • Workforce development organisations.
  • Teams developing education datasets.
  • Collaborations involving researchers, educators, technologists and community organisations.

Applicants should consult the official competition rules and the specific requirements for their preferred track before preparing a submission. The overview page alone does not provide a complete list of all eligibility conditions, submission requirements, funding amounts per award or selection criteria.

Geographic Eligibility

The 2027 Tools Competition overview describes its goal as supporting learning, teaching and opportunity needs in real-world settings and refers to learners worldwide. However, the provided overview does not explicitly state a complete country-by-country eligibility list or a definitive nationality restriction.

Therefore, individuals and organisations from outside the United States should review the official eligibility requirements, rules and submission information to confirm whether they can apply. Applicants from Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, the Caribbean, Oceania and other regions should not assume eligibility solely based on the global focus of the competition.

The official eligibility quiz and rules should be consulted for clarification:

  • Check eligibility through the official eligibility quiz
  • Read the official competition rules

Application and Submission Information

The competition’s official website provides a Submit Here link for applicants who are ready to submit their proposals.

Applicants should review the relevant track page and official rules before submitting. They should ensure that their proposal addresses the specific problem, target users, expected impact and implementation context associated with the selected track.

A strong submission may benefit from including the following information, subject to the official application requirements:

  1. Problem statement
    Clearly explain the educational or workforce challenge the proposed tool intends to address.
  2. Target users
    Identify the learners, educators, institutions, researchers or other groups that will use or benefit from the solution.
  3. Proposed solution
    Describe how the tool, platform, dataset or infrastructure will work.
  4. Evidence and rationale
    Explain the research, learning science, user feedback or practical evidence supporting the approach.
  5. Expected outcomes
    Describe how the proposed solution could improve learning, teaching, assessment, career navigation or education research.
  6. Implementation plan
    Explain how the solution will be developed, tested, introduced or used in real-world settings.
  7. Safety and privacy measures
    Describe how the proposal will address data protection, responsible AI, accessibility, fairness and user safety.
  8. Sustainability plan
    Explain how the tool or dataset can be maintained, improved and used over time.

Applicants should rely on the official submission form and rules for the precise format, documentation and information required.

Submit a proposal through the official competition website:
Submit to the 2027 Tools Competition

Competition Information Session

The organisers have announced an information session for prospective applicants.

Interested participants can register for the information session scheduled for:

Date: September 15, 2026

The session may provide additional guidance about the competition, its tracks, eligibility, application process and expectations for proposals.

Register for the 2027 Tools Competition information session

Applicants should confirm the session time, format and registration requirements through the official registration page.

Application Deadline

The provided competition overview announces that the 2027 Tools Competition is live, but it does not state a final application deadline.

Application Deadline: Not specified in the provided competition overview.

Applicants should visit the official submission page, official rules and relevant track pages for the latest deadline information. Since competition timelines may be updated, prospective applicants should avoid relying on unofficial deadlines or outdated announcements.

Organisers and Programme Partners

The 2027 Tools Competition is supported and organised by two organisations:

Renaissance Philanthropy

Renaissance Philanthropy is identified as the programme behind the Tools Competition. The organisation supports initiatives intended to advance innovation and address important challenges through philanthropic investment and strategic programmes.

Visit Renaissance Philanthropy

The Learning Agency

The Learning Agency is responsible for organising the Tools Competition. The organisation works on initiatives related to learning, education, research, innovation and the development of tools that can improve learning outcomes.

Visit The Learning Agency

How to Prepare a Strong Proposal

Applicants can improve their readiness by taking the following steps:

1. Select the most appropriate track

Review all four tracks and identify which one best matches the purpose of the proposed tool or dataset. Avoid submitting a general idea that does not clearly align with a competition priority.

2. Define the problem precisely

Explain the problem in clear language. Identify who experiences the problem, why it matters and what limitations exist in current approaches.

3. Demonstrate user need

Use research, interviews, surveys, pilot findings, classroom experience or other evidence to show that the problem is real and significant.

4. Explain what makes the solution different

Describe how the proposed tool improves on existing approaches. The difference may involve better accessibility, stronger evidence, improved usability, greater inclusiveness, better data quality or more effective implementation.

5. Include evidence of feasibility

Explain whether the team has already developed a prototype, conducted a pilot, tested the concept or gathered feedback from potential users. If the solution is still at an early stage, clearly describe the next steps.

6. Address responsible innovation

Explain how the proposal will handle privacy, safety, fairness, accessibility, transparency and responsible use of artificial intelligence or data.

7. Plan for real-world adoption

Consider how the tool will be used by schools, educators, learners, institutions, researchers or other stakeholders. A proposal should demonstrate awareness of practical constraints such as cost, training, infrastructure and user support.

8. Review the official rules

Before submission, applicants should read the official rules, confirm eligibility and ensure that their proposal meets the required format and criteria.

Conclusion

The 2027 Tools Competition presents a major opportunity for innovators, researchers, education technology developers, organisations and data specialists working to improve learning, teaching and access to opportunity.

Through its four tracks—Strengthening Teaching, Reimagining Assessment, Navigating Postsecondary Learning and Work, and Building Better Datasets—the competition seeks solutions that address real challenges across K–12 education, postsecondary learning, career transitions and education research.

The competition’s focus extends beyond technological novelty. It encourages tools that are evidence-informed, practical, inclusive, safe, privacy-conscious and capable of producing meaningful outcomes in real learning environments.

Potential applicants should carefully review the relevant track, complete the official eligibility check, read the competition rules and confirm the final submission deadline. The information provided in the competition overview does not specify a final deadline, so applicants should consult the official website for the latest updates.

item.content:encoded:
The University of Saskatchewan (USask) Toxicology Graduate Program is accepting applications for its research-intensive Master of Science (M.Sc.) and Doctor of Philosophy (Ph.D.) programs in Toxicology in Canada. The program is particularly attractive to students interested in environmental health, contaminant science, ecological risk assessment, human health, wildlife toxicology, analytical toxicology, molecular toxicology, and related scientific fields.

One of the most important features of the program is its funding structure. The University of Saskatchewan states that all graduate students accepted into the Toxicology Graduate Program are guaranteed funding, with current minimum stipends of CAD 23,000 for master’s students and CAD 26,000 for doctoral students. The Toxicology Centre separately describes accepted students as receiving full funding once they have secured a research supervisor and satisfied admission requirements.

Another major advantage is application flexibility. There is no fixed application deadline for the Toxicology M.Sc. or Ph.D. programs. Applications are accepted continuously throughout the year, and students may start their studies in January, May, or September.

Both Canadian and international applicants can apply, subject to academic, English-language, research, and admission requirements.

About the University of Saskatchewan Toxicology Graduate Program

The Toxicology Graduate Program is an interdisciplinary research program at the University of Saskatchewan. It offers research-based M.Sc. and Ph.D. pathways designed to prepare students to investigate the effects of contaminants and potentially harmful physical or chemical agents on human beings, animals, ecosystems, and biological systems.

Research and postgraduate education in toxicology are coordinated through the University of Saskatchewan Toxicology Centre and involve academics from numerous university departments as well as scientists from government research institutions. This multidisciplinary structure allows graduate students to work across conventional disciplinary boundaries rather than being restricted to one narrow scientific field.

The Toxicology Centre’s broader mission is to train highly capable toxicologists who can contribute to emerging human and environmental health challenges while strengthening research, public engagement, technical outreach, and international leadership in toxicology.

Degrees Available

Applicants can pursue either a Master of Science or Doctor of Philosophy degree.

Program Typical duration Format Delivery
M.Sc. in Toxicology Approximately 2 years Research/thesis-based In person
Ph.D. in Toxicology Approximately 3–4 years; USask lists 4 years as the expected length Research/dissertation-based In person

The program is therefore designed primarily for students seeking advanced scientific research training rather than a classroom-only postgraduate qualification.

Why Study Toxicology at the University of Saskatchewan?

Toxicology sits at the intersection of environmental science, biology, chemistry, medicine, veterinary science, ecology, public health, and risk assessment. Students can investigate how pollutants and contaminants move through environmental systems, how living organisms respond to chemical exposure, how toxic substances affect human and animal health, and how scientific evidence can inform environmental regulation and risk management.

USask highlights three broad strengths of its program: exposure to numerous areas of toxicology, interdisciplinary research involving university faculty and government scientists, and preparation for careers in government, consulting, industry, public health, and academia.

The program has a particularly strong environmental and aquatic toxicology component, while faculty research spans a considerably broader spectrum.

Toxicology Research Areas and Specializations

Depending on supervisor availability and the applicant’s research interests, potential areas of graduate specialization include:

  • Analytical toxicology
  • Aquatic toxicology
  • Ecotoxicology
  • Immunotoxicology
  • Molecular and biochemical toxicology
  • Nutritional toxicology
  • Soil toxicology
  • Environmental contaminant research
  • Ecological and human-health risk assessment
  • Veterinary toxicology
  • Human toxicology
  • Wildlife toxicology
  • Forensic toxicology
  • Radiation toxicology
  • Molecular biology related to toxicological mechanisms
  • Contaminant exposure and environmental chemistry

The official University Catalogue confirms that the interdisciplinary program extends across areas such as analytical, aquatic, ecological, forensic, immunological, nutritional, radiation, veterinary, and wildlife toxicology.

Examples of Research Available Through USask Toxicology

The breadth of the faculty provides potential research opportunities involving topics such as heavy-metal neurotoxicity, exposure modelling, contaminant effects on aquatic organisms, livestock toxicology, environmental pollutants, computational chemistry, reproductive and developmental toxicology, food-web contamination, biomagnification, pesticides, northern ecosystems, metal bioaccumulation, selenium and human health, emerging contaminants, soil ecotoxicology, air pollution, cardiovascular effects, environmental genetics, DNA damage, and chemical mixtures.

This interdisciplinary environment is particularly valuable for students whose research interests cross environmental, biological, chemical, veterinary, or human-health disciplines.

Research Supervisors

The University strongly recommends identifying and contacting a prospective supervisor before submitting an application.

Applicants should review the faculty members associated with the Toxicology Graduate Program and identify researchers whose expertise aligns closely with their proposed area of study. Prospective students are encouraged to contact an appropriate faculty member with information about their academic background, research interests, and proposed graduate goals.

If the faculty member is accepting new students and considers the applicant potentially suitable, the prospective supervisor may then advise the student to proceed with the formal application. Supervisor approval is described by the program as highly recommended before applying.

This step should not be treated as a formality. For a research-based master’s or Ph.D., the fit between the applicant’s interests and the supervisor’s active research program can be central to admission, research funding, and successful completion of the degree.

Guaranteed Funding for Accepted Toxicology Graduate Students

Funding is one of the strongest aspects of this opportunity.

According to the official graduate-program page, all graduate students are guaranteed funding if accepted into the Toxicology program. The minimum stipend levels currently stated are:

Degree Minimum stipend
M.Sc. CAD 23,000
Ph.D. CAD 26,000

The Toxicology Centre further states that once a student has been accepted by a supervisor for their research program and has met the admission requirements, graduate students are guaranteed full funding. Basic health-insurance coverage is also identified as guaranteed by the Centre.

Applicants should understand an important distinction: guaranteed funding does not mean that tuition and university fees disappear. Students are still assessed tuition and student fees. The stipend and other funding support should therefore be considered alongside the actual cost of enrollment.

Additional Scholarships and Awards

Graduate students may also have access to other University of Saskatchewan funding opportunities. Across the university, the College of Graduate and Postdoctoral Studies administers more than CAD 14 million in scholarships annually, with funding originating from governments, university programs, donors, and individual academic units.

The Toxicology Centre also lists program-specific awards and scholarships. These include opportunities such as an entrance scholarship for incoming M.Sc. and Ph.D. students, academic awards, research-presentation travel funding, and a Student Support Fund. Individual awards have their own eligibility criteria and deadlines and should not be confused with the standard guaranteed funding package attached to admission.

M.Sc. in Toxicology Admission Requirements

Applicants seeking admission to the master’s program must generally hold a relevant undergraduate qualification.

For the Toxicology M.Sc., USask requires a four-year honours degree or equivalent from a recognized university or college in an academic discipline relevant to the intended field of study, together with a minimum cumulative weighted average equivalent to 70% in the final two years of study. Proof of English-language proficiency may also be required.

The Toxicology Centre provides additional academic guidance, indicating that applicants should normally have an undergraduate background in the life or natural sciences. Preparation in biology, chemistry, biochemistry, physiology, and statistics is particularly relevant, while previous study in environmental chemistry, ecology, pharmacology, or toxicology can be advantageous.

Meeting the minimum academic threshold does not automatically guarantee admission.

Ph.D. in Toxicology Admission Requirements

Applicants seeking direct admission to the Ph.D. program normally require a master’s degree or equivalent from a recognized institution in a discipline relevant to toxicology.

The applicant must also generally have a cumulative weighted average of at least 70% on the USask grading-equivalent scale in the relevant master’s coursework. English-language proficiency requirements may apply to international applicants and applicants whose first language is not English.

As with the master’s program, applicants should also demonstrate the capacity for independent academic research and advanced graduate study.

M.Sc. Degree Requirements

The M.Sc. is a research-based program. According to the 2026–2027 University Catalogue, students must maintain continuous registration in the required research course and complete relevant graduate ethics, seminar, research, and academic-course requirements.

The program includes a minimum of nine credit units of core coursework, selected in consultation with the student’s advisory committee and approved by the graduate chair. Additional ethics requirements apply where human or animal research is involved.

The degree is therefore structured around both formal graduate study and substantial independent research.

Ph.D. Degree Requirements

The Ph.D. places greater emphasis on independent original research.

Doctoral students must maintain continuous registration in their designated research course, complete required research and ethics components, participate in the toxicology seminar requirement, and complete at least six credit units selected in consultation with the advisory committee.

Ph.D. candidates must also successfully complete a doctoral candidacy assessment and dissertation defense.

English-Language Requirements for International Applicants

Because instruction and examination at the University of Saskatchewan are conducted in English, applicants may be required to establish English proficiency.

The university’s current general graduate thresholds include the following:

Test Minimum graduate-level requirement
IELTS Academic Overall 6.5, with no component below 6.0
TOEFL iBT 86 overall with at least 19 in each area for the applicable scoring format; USask also publishes requirements for the revised TOEFL scale used for tests dated January 21, 2026 onward
Cambridge C1 Advanced 176 overall
Duolingo English Test 120 overall, with at least 100 in each area
PTE Academic 63 overall, with at least 59 in each area
CAEL 70 overall, with individual scores of at least 60

USask may also recognize qualifying previous study conducted entirely in English, subject to university and academic-unit rules. English tests generally remain valid for 24 months and must still be valid when the student begins the graduate program.

Applicants should verify the current test requirements immediately before applying because language-testing systems and university thresholds can change.

Tuition for M.Sc. Students in 2026–2027

The current posted tuition for thesis/project-based master’s students is:

2026–2027 term Canadian students International students
September–December CAD 1,902 CAD 4,279
January–April CAD 1,902 CAD 4,279
May–August CAD 1,902 CAD 4,279
Academic-year total CAD 5,706 CAD 12,837

These amounts do not include applicable student fees.

Tuition for Ph.D. Students in 2026–2027

For doctoral students, domestic and international students currently pay the same published Ph.D. tuition rate:

2026–2027 term Tuition
September–December CAD 1,879
January–April CAD 1,879
May–August CAD 1,879
Academic-year total CAD 5,637

This equal domestic/international Ph.D. tuition structure can be particularly significant for international doctoral applicants.

Additional Student Fees

Full-time on-campus students may also be assessed fees supporting services such as health and dental coverage, transit, and other student services.

For the 2026–2027 academic year, the program page currently lists student fees of CAD 617.36 for Fall 2026, CAD 854.96 for Winter 2027, and CAD 46.75 each for Spring and Summer 2027, subject to university policies and the student’s enrollment circumstances.

Applicants should therefore budget using both tuition and student fees rather than relying only on the tuition figure.

Application Deadline

There is no fixed application deadline.

The University of Saskatchewan states that Toxicology applications are accepted on a year-round, continual basis. Students can begin the program in:

January, May, or September.

Because a research supervisor is highly recommended and international applicants may require significant time for study-permit processing, applying well ahead of the intended start term is prudent even though there is no formal program deadline.

Application Process

A prospective applicant should first investigate the available research areas and identify an appropriate Toxicology faculty member whose work aligns with their interests. After discussing potential supervision, the applicant can submit the formal University of Saskatchewan graduate application.

The online application requests personal details, the applicant’s complete post-secondary academic history, and information for three referees. Two referees must be academic contacts, while the third may be either academic or professional. The university estimates that the initial online application takes approximately 30 minutes and allows applicants to save their progress before submission.

Application Fee

The current non-refundable graduate application fee is:

Canadian/domestic applicant: CAD 125

International applicant: CAD 145

The application will not proceed to processing until the required fee has been paid.

Documents Applicants Should Prepare

After submitting the online application and paying the fee, applicants receive access to the Supplemental Items & Documents section of the application system.

Applicants are initially required to upload unofficial PDF transcripts from each post-secondary institution they attended. Documents must include the institution’s grading information or legend, and all pages of each transcript should be combined into one PDF. Transcripts issued in languages other than English need a certified English translation. Official transcripts are generally requested from applicants who receive an offer of admission.

Depending on the applicant and program assessment, additional documentation can include a current CV or résumé, a statement or letter of intent describing experience and interest in toxicology, English-language test evidence where required, and letters of recommendation.

What to Include in a Strong Statement of Intent

For a research-based program of this nature, applicants should avoid sending a generic statement that simply says they are interested in science or environmental protection.

A strong statement should clearly establish the applicant’s academic preparation, previous research or laboratory exposure, proposed area of toxicology, methodological interests, reasons for choosing USask, and the connection between those interests and a potential supervisor.

Applicants should also explain how their previous academic or professional experience prepares them for independent graduate research and what they hope to accomplish through the M.Sc. or Ph.D.

International Students and Canadian Study Permits

International students are explicitly considered within the University’s graduate admission process.

For current Canadian immigration procedures reflected on the USask website, master’s and doctoral students applying for a Canadian study permit do not require a Provincial Attestation Letter (PAL). USask advises international applicants to review current federal study-permit requirements before applying because immigration policies can change independently of university admission rules.

Admission to the university and approval of a Canadian study permit remain separate processes.

Indigenous and Under-Represented Applicants

The Toxicology Graduate Program specifically states that it encourages applications from Indigenous students and individuals from under-represented groups.

USask explains that incorporating diverse perspectives and knowledge systems can improve the relevance and impact of environmental and toxicological research.

This is an encouragement and inclusion statement, however, rather than a restriction: the general Toxicology M.Sc. and Ph.D. programs are not limited to applicants from a particular racial or ethnic group.

Career Opportunities After a Toxicology Graduate Degree

The interdisciplinary nature of toxicology can prepare graduates for positions across environmental science, regulatory work, research, industry, health, and academia.

USask specifically identifies potential employment pathways in government, environmental consulting, industry, public health, and academic research. The Toxicology Centre also states that its graduates are prepared for careers with government agencies, consulting organizations, industrial employers, universities, and further postgraduate research.

Career possibilities can vary considerably depending on the student’s research specialization, laboratory capabilities, quantitative skills, publications, professional network, and regulatory expertise.

Key Program Information at a Glance

Item Details
University University of Saskatchewan
Location Saskatchewan, Canada
Field Toxicology
Degrees M.Sc. and Ph.D.
Study format Research-intensive, in person
Expected M.Sc. length Approximately 2 years
Expected Ph.D. length Approximately 4 years
M.Sc. minimum funding CAD 23,000
Ph.D. minimum funding CAD 26,000
Funding Guaranteed for accepted Toxicology graduate students
International applicants Eligible
Application deadline No fixed deadline; applications accepted year-round
Entry terms January, May, September
Supervisor Approval/contact highly recommended before applying
M.Sc. academic threshold At least 70% USask equivalent in final two years
Ph.D. academic threshold Relevant master’s degree and at least 70% USask equivalent
Application fee CAD 125 domestic; CAD 145 international

Important Funding Clarification

Applicants should not interpret the phrase “guaranteed funding” as meaning that there are no costs associated with studying at USask.

The Toxicology program provides a guaranteed minimum stipend for accepted students, while the university separately charges tuition and student fees. Prospective students should therefore calculate the net financial position after tuition, university fees, living costs, insurance arrangements, transportation, housing, and other expenses.

This distinction is especially important for international M.Sc. students because the published international master’s tuition is higher than the domestic master’s rate.

Conclusion

The University of Saskatchewan Toxicology M.Sc. and Ph.D. programs offer a strong opportunity for students seeking advanced, interdisciplinary research training in environmental, human, wildlife, analytical, aquatic, molecular, veterinary, and ecological toxicology.

The combination of guaranteed graduate funding, minimum stipends of CAD 23,000 for M.Sc. students and CAD 26,000 for Ph.D. students, year-round applications, multiple annual entry points, and eligibility for international students makes the program particularly noteworthy for prospective researchers seeking graduate study in Canada.

Prospective applicants should begin by identifying an appropriate research supervisor, assessing whether their academic background aligns with the program, preparing a focused research-oriented statement of intent, and completing the formal USask graduate application.

There is no fixed application deadline, but applicants should apply sufficiently early for their intended January, May, or September start date, particularly if international study-permit processing will be required.

Official University of Saskatchewan Toxicology Graduate Program

The Global Health Emerging Scholars (GHES) Fellowship 2027–28 is now accepting applications from emerging health researchers interested in advanced, mentored training in global health research. Supported by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) through the Fogarty International Center (FIC), the fellowship provides a 12-month research training experience designed to prepare the next generation of researchers and health professionals to address major and emerging global health challenges.

The GHES Fellowship brings together a consortium of leading U.S. universities, including Yale University, Stanford University, the University of California, Berkeley, and the University of Arizona, together with partner institutions in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs).

The program offers research training opportunities across 15 countries, providing fellows with the opportunity to work within international research environments while receiving mentorship from experienced global health researchers.

For scholars seeking to develop a career in global health research, epidemiology, public health, medicine, disease prevention, health systems, environmental health, or related fields, the GHES Fellowship provides an opportunity to gain specialized research experience, strengthen academic and professional networks, and contribute to research addressing population health challenges.

What Is the Global Health Emerging Scholars Fellowship?

The Global Health Emerging Scholars (GHES) Fellowship is a 12-month, NIH-supported, mentored global health research training program.

The fellowship is designed to improve population health by developing researchers who can conduct rigorous research and contribute to solutions for pressing health challenges around the world.

The program is part of the Global Health Program for Fellows and Scholars/Launching Future Leaders in Global Health Research Training Program (LAUNCH), which is sponsored by the Fogarty International Center and collaborating institutes and centers at the NIH.

The fellowship year typically runs from July through June and provides participants with opportunities to undertake research training through a network of partner institutions in 15 LMICs.

Rather than focusing solely on classroom-based education, the program emphasizes mentored research training. Fellows are connected with experienced faculty members and research institutions whose work aligns with their research interests.

This structure allows participants to develop their research skills while gaining experience in international and multidisciplinary global health settings.

GHES Fellowship 2027–28 Application Deadline

The application for the 2027–28 GHES Fellowship year is currently open.

Deadline: October 1, 2026, at 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time.

Applicants are encouraged to review the eligibility requirements carefully before submitting an application, particularly because eligibility requirements differ between U.S.-based applicants and applicants from LMICs.

Who Is the GHES Fellowship Designed For?

The fellowship is intended for emerging researchers at the predoctoral and postdoctoral levels.

There are three major applicant categories:

  1. U.S. postdoctoral scholars
  2. U.S.-based doctoral or professional students
  3. Postdoctoral scholars based in eligible low- and middle-income countries

The precise requirements depend on the applicant’s academic status, citizenship or residency, institutional affiliation, and doctoral or professional qualifications.

U.S. Postdoctoral Fellowship Eligibility

U.S.-based postdoctoral applicants may be eligible if they meet the program’s requirements.

Applicants must generally:

  • Be a U.S. citizen or U.S. resident.
  • Provide a green card number where required for the application.
  • Have completed a qualifying doctoral degree within the past five years or be on track to complete the doctoral degree by June 2027.
  • Obtain endorsement from appropriate GHES mentors.
  • Have research interests that align with the expertise of available GHES mentors.

Applicants may come from any U.S. academic institution, rather than being restricted exclusively to Yale University, Stanford University, UC Berkeley, or the University of Arizona.

However, applicants who are not already affiliated with one of the consortium universities must obtain approval from the GHES Program Manager before applying.

Such applicants are expected to provide information including:

  • Their curriculum vitae.
  • A description of their research interests.
  • Potential GHES mentor(s) whose research aligns with their interests.
  • An NIH biosketch where required.
  • Information demonstrating that they have contacted potential mentors.

The doctoral degrees considered for eligibility include, among others:

  • PhD
  • MD
  • DVM
  • DrPH
  • PharmD

Applicants should carefully confirm whether their specific degree and academic status meet the current eligibility requirements.

U.S. Doctoral Student Fellowship Eligibility

The GHES program also provides opportunities for eligible U.S.-based doctoral and professional students.

Applicants in this category must generally:

  • Be a U.S. citizen or U.S. resident.
  • Be enrolled at UC Berkeley, the University of Arizona, Yale University, or Stanford University, or establish an appropriate affiliation with one of these institutions for the fellowship.
  • Be advanced-candidacy doctoral students or eligible professional students.
  • Professional students may include students pursuing degrees such as:
    • MD
    • DDS
    • DVM
    • PharmD
    • Other qualifying professional degrees.
  • Professional students must generally have completed at least three years of professional schooling.

The program is therefore particularly relevant to advanced doctoral and professional students who are preparing to develop research careers in global health.

LMIC Postdoctoral Fellowship Eligibility

The GHES Fellowship also welcomes eligible postdoctoral scholars from low- and middle-income countries.

For this category, applicants must generally:

  • Be a citizen of a low- or middle-income country as defined by the World Bank.
  • Have received a qualifying doctoral degree within the previous five years.
  • Be affiliated with one of the GHES partner LMIC institutions.
  • Obtain endorsement from appropriate GHES mentors.
  • Have research interests that align with the available research training opportunities and mentors.

Qualifying doctoral degrees can include:

  • MBBS
  • MMed
  • PhD
  • Other qualifying doctoral or professional degrees.

Importantly, the LMIC postdoctoral category requires a doctoral or professional degree. A master’s degree alone does not meet the stated requirement for this category.

Countries and Regions Represented by the GHES Network

The GHES consortium operates through collaborations involving institutions in 15 LMICs.

The network spans multiple geographical regions, including:

  • Africa
  • Latin America
  • The Caribbean
  • South and Southeast Asia
  • The Middle East
  • Eastern Europe
  • Oceania

This international structure gives fellows access to research environments addressing health issues in different populations and geographic contexts.

The program’s partner-site model is particularly important because applicants are expected to identify research sites and mentors that align with their proposed research interests.

GHES Fellowship Research Sites Associated With Stanford
